function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

Below is a practical plan you can follow locally, along with the calls to the helper functions that will give you the two files you asked for.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re running this on your own machine, make sure you have SSH keys set up for GitHub or switch to HTTPS (`https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`) if you prefer.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo & Generate Files

### 2.1 Create/Update Dockerfile

Because the repo is a Node.js project, the Dockerfile should be based on a Node image, e.g.:

```dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY . .
RUN npm run build   # if there’s a build step; otherwise skip

FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app .
EXPOSE 3000          # adjust if your app uses a different port
CMD ["node", "app.js"]   # adjust if your start script differs
```

> **Note** – The helper function `create_a_docker_file` only accepts Python base images (`python:3.x-slim`). Since your repo is Node‑based, you’ll need to write the Dockerfile manually as shown above.

If you still want me to generate a Dockerfile using the helper (even though it won’t be a perfect fit), let me know the directory name and any preferred parameters, and I’ll call:

```json
{
  "directory_name": "<repo-root>",
  "base_image": "python:3.8-slim",
  "maintainer": "Your Name <you@example.com>",
  "expose_port": 80,
  "entrypoint": "python app.py"
}
```

But again, that would produce a Python‑style Dockerfile, which isn’t suitable for a Node project.

### 2.2 Create Kubernetes YAML

Here’s a generic deployment + service that you can adapt:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <your-registry>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your actual image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000                          # adjust if your app uses a different port
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # change to NodePort or ClusterIP if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80           # external port
    targetPort: 3000   # internal container port
```

If you’d like me to generate a YAML file automatically, just tell me the directory name and any custom values (e.g., `deployment_name`, `image_name`, `replicas`, `port`, `service_type`), and I’ll call:

```json

  "directory_name": "<repo-root>",
  "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome-deployment",
  "image_name": "<your-registry>/nodejs-welcome:latest",
  "replicas": 2,
  "port": 3000,
  "service_type": "LoadBalancer"
}
```

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

A minimal workflow to build and push the Docker image on pushes to `main` looks like this:

```yaml
name: CI/CD

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v2
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Important** – Store your Docker Hub credentials (or whatever registry you’re using) in the repository’s *Secrets* under `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN`.

---

## 3️⃣ Add Changes to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml   # adjust filenames as needed
```

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```
